chunks: "SPI stands for Serial Peripheral Interface. It's a synchronous, full-duplex serial bus where one master talks to one or more slaves, originally from Motorola.
It uses four signals: SCLK, the clock from the master; MOSI, master out slave in; MISO, master in slave out; and CS, chip select, which the master pulls low to pick a slave and frame the transfer.
The neat way to understand it is as two shift registers connected in a ring. The master has one, the slave has one.
On every clock edge, the master shifts one bit out on MOSI while the slave shifts one bit out on MISO, and each side shifts the other's bit in.
After eight clocks the two bytes have been swapped.
That's why it's full-duplex: sending and receiving happen at the same time, and a read is just 'send a dummy byte and look at what came back'.

What it doesn't have is anything fancy: no addresses, because the chip select does that; no acknowledge, so the master doesn't know if anyone is listening; and no formal standard, just conventions like the four clock modes.
In exchange, since the drivers are push-pull and there are no pull-ups, it runs at tens of megahertz, which is why flash, displays, ADCs and SD cards use it."
